## Verdict

missing

## Bearer

DataLayerMessageChannel.send — core-sync/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/sync/transport/MessageChannel.kt
WearableProfileSyncTransport.send — core-sync/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/sync/transport/WearableProfileSyncTransport.kt
WearableRecordedRaceTransport.send — core-sync/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/sync/transport/WearableRecordedRaceTransport.kt
WearableRecordedRaceAckTransport.send — core-sync/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/sync/transport/WearableRecordedRaceAckTransport.kt
HrHistoryReaderImpl.bpmValuesOverLast12Months — app-phone/src/main/java/com/mgilli/hyroxtracker/health/HrHistoryReaderImpl.kt

## Trigger

Each of the five methods is already called from its existing production
flow — a sync push, an acknowledgement, or the profile screen's history
read. The catch sites fire on the exception the underlying call raises;
nothing new needs to start observing them — observed.

## Today

All five `catch (other: Exception)` blocks discard what they caught and
return a plain failure value with nothing recorded: the four transports
(`DataLayerMessageChannel.send`, `WearableProfileSyncTransport.send`,
`WearableRecordedRaceTransport.send`, `WearableRecordedRaceAckTransport.send`)
return `false`, and `HrHistoryReaderImpl.bpmValuesOverLast12Months` returns
`emptyList()`. No `Log` call, no `Timber` call and no logging utility of any
kind exists anywhere in the project — `android.util.Log`, `Timber.` and
`logger.` all return zero matches across every module — so there is nothing
to widen; the fix introduces the first logging calls the codebase makes.
An unreachable node, a `PayloadCodec.encode`/`decode` failure, a revoked
Health Connect permission and a corrupt stored record are today
indistinguishable from outside any of these five methods.

Separately, in `WearableProfileSyncTransport.send` and
`WearableRecordedRaceTransport.send`, the single `try` block wraps both
`PayloadCodec.encode(payload)` and `channel.send(...)`:

```
override suspend fun send(payload: ProfileSyncPayload): Boolean = try {
    channel.send(PATH, PayloadCodec.encode(payload))
} catch (other: Exception) {
    false
}
```

`PayloadCodec.encode` serialises the snapshot with `ObjectOutputStream`
and can raise on a data-model problem (e.g. a non-serialisable field);
that failure is caught by the same block as a connection failure from
`channel.send`, so both are reported as `false` alike — a data-model bug
reads as a network drop. `DataLayerMessageChannel.send` itself never calls
`PayloadCodec` — it only receives an already-encoded `ByteArray` — so the
catch that needs to stop covering encoding sits in the two payload
transports, not in `MessageChannel`. `WearableRecordedRaceAckTransport.send`
does not call `PayloadCodec` at all (it builds its own `ByteBuffer`), so it
is unaffected by this second point.

## Expected

Each of the five catch sites logs what it caught before returning its
existing failure value, at a level matching how much it matters — an
unreachable node or a mid-sync cancellation-adjacent failure is routine
and logs low, a `PayloadCodec` serialisation failure or a corrupt stored
record is a data-model defect and logs high, a revoked permission is an
expected, user-facing condition and logs accordingly. None of them changes
its return type or its contract with its caller.

In `WearableProfileSyncTransport.send` and `WearableRecordedRaceTransport.send`,
the call to `PayloadCodec.encode(payload)` moves out of the `try` that
guards `channel.send`, so an encoding failure is distinguished — logged
and handled on its own terms — from a delivery failure, and the catch
around `channel.send` covers the send alone.
